groups.title: After the trials
groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

parts.context: A lecturer describes the stages of vaccine development.

transcript.text: Good morning. Today I'd like to explain how a new vaccine is developed. It's a process that most people only hear about in the news, so I want to show you the steps and the reasons behind them.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: Many people imagine that scientists simply invent a vaccine in a few weeks. In reality, a typical programme takes ten years or more, which is why the rapid development of some recent vaccines was such an exceptional achievement, built on decades of earlier research.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: The first stage is research in the laboratory, where scientists study the structure of the virus or bacterium. Their aim is to find a part of it that the immune system can recognise.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: Next, a candidate vaccine is tested on animals, usually mice, to check that it triggers a response from the immune system and doesn't cause obvious harm.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: If the results are promising, the vaccine moves to Phase One trials, involving a small group of between twenty and eighty volunteers, mainly to check safety.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: Phase Two expands to several hundred people, and the main goal is to find the correct dose. Researchers also look for differences between age groups.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: Phase Three is the largest, with thousands of participants, half receiving the vaccine and half a placebo, so that researchers can compare the two groups and measure how well the vaccine protects people.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: Each phase must be successful before the next one can begin, and many candidate vaccines fail along the way. It is normal for a company to start with dozens of ideas and end up with only one or two that are safe and effective enough to continue.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: Even after the trials, approval is not automatic. Regulators examine the data for several months, looking at both effectiveness and safety before they allow the vaccine to be used.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: Once approved, the vaccine must be manufactured on a huge scale. Many vaccines need to be stored at very low temperatures, some as cold as minus seventy degrees, which creates serious logistical problems.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: Quality control is also demanding. Every batch is tested before it leaves the factory, and a small change in the production process can mean that the whole batch must be thrown away, which is one reason why supplies can be limited.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: Distribution is another challenge, especially in rural areas where roads are poor and electricity is unreliable. Health workers sometimes carry vaccines in special cool boxes on motorbikes.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: Monitoring continues after the programme begins. Doctors record any side effects, which are usually mild, such as a sore arm, and report them to a central database.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: These reports are reviewed by independent experts, who look for any unusual pattern. If a rare problem appears, the programme can be paused while investigators decide whether the vaccine was the cause.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: Finally, public trust is vital. Even an excellent vaccine will not protect a community if too few people accept it, so clear communication from trusted local figures such as doctors and teachers makes a big difference.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: It is worth remembering that the same steps apply to vaccines for many different diseases, from influenza to malaria, although each disease brings its own scientific difficulties.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN

transcript.text: So you can see that a vaccine is the result of many years of careful work by thousands of people. Thank you for listening.
transcript.speaker: DR KHAN
